parts.label: (a)
parts.text: For a progressive wave on a stretched string, state what is meant by *amplitude*.
hints: Hint 1: Picture one small piece of the string vibrating up and down about its rest position - what is the furthest distance it moves from the centre?
parts.proper_answer: The maximum displacement of a point on the string from its equilibrium position.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Amplitude Really Means**
Imagine the string at rest as a straight horizontal line. When the wave passes, each point moves up and down. Amplitude is simply how far that point gets from the middle at its furthest point, on either side.

Step 2: **Precise Definition**
So you can say $$\text{amplitude} = \text{maximum displacement from equilibrium}$$ It is not the distance from trough to crest, that is twice the amplitude.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Light from a laser has a wavelength of $690\text{ nm}$ in a vacuum.

Calculate the period of the light wave.
hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about how fast this light wave is travelling and what two wave quantities link speed to the time for one oscillation.
Hint 2: Convert the 690 nm wavelength into metres and remember that frequency and period are reciprocals of each other.
Hint 3: Combine the ideas to first find the frequency from speed and wavelength, then invert it to get the very short period.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking Speed, Wavelength and Period**
For any wave, speed tells you how many wavelengths pass per second. That rate is the frequency $f$. In symbols $$v = f\lambda$$ and period $T$ is the time for one oscillation $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ Combining gives $$v = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$

Step 2: **Putting In Numbers For Light**
In vacuum, light travels at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8} \text{ m s}^{-1}$. Convert wavelength: $$\lambda = 690 \text{ nm} = 690 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$$ Rearrange for $T$: $$T = \frac{\lambda}{c}$$ $$T = \frac{690 \times 10^{-9}}{3.00 \times 10^{8}}$$

Step 3: **Final Value**
$$T = 2.3 \times 10^{-15} \text{ s}$$ This extremely small time makes sense because visible light oscillates about $10^{14}$ times per second.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem:
A two-source interference experiment uses the arrangement shown in Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1 (not to scale)

Light from a laser is incident normally on a double slit. A screen is parallel to the double slit.

Interference fringes are seen on the screen at distance $D$ from the double slit. The separation of the centres of the slits is $a$. The light has wavelength $\lambda$.

The separation $x$ of the centres of adjacent bright fringes is measured for different values of distance $D$.

The variation with $D$ of $x$ is shown in Fig. 5.2.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

Fig. 5.2

The gradient of the graph is $G$.
parts.text: Determine an expression, in terms of $G$ and $\lambda$, for the separation $a$ of the slits.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what controls how widely spaced the bright fringes are when you change wavelength, slit separation and screen distance.
Hint 2: Compare the standard fringe spacing relation with the straight-line form $x = G D$ to see what the gradient $G$ must represent, then rearrange for $a$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Fringe Spacing Formula**
For double-slit interference with coherent light, the separation of adjacent bright fringes is $$x = \frac{\lambda D}{a}$$ where $D$ is slit to screen distance and $a$ is slit separation. So $x$ is directly proportional to $D$.

Step 2: **Matching To The Graph Gradient**
The graph of $x$ against $D$ is a straight line through the origin with gradient $G$: $$G = \frac{x}{D}$$ From the fringe formula $$\frac{x}{D} = \frac{\lambda}{a}$$ so $$G = \frac{\lambda}{a}$$ Rearranging for $a$: $$a = \frac{\lambda}{G}$$

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
The experiment is repeated with slits of separation $2a$. The wavelength of the light is unchanged.

On Fig. 5.2, sketch a graph to show the results of this experiment.

markscheme_points.text: straight line from origin always below printed line
line is half the height of printed line at maximum

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the fringe spacing $x$ for a fixed $D$ if the slits are moved further apart while $\lambda$ stays the same.
Hint 2: Use your expression $a = \lambda / G$ to work out the new gradient when $a$ becomes $2a$, and think about the shape and starting point of the new line.
parts.proper_answer: Straight line through origin with half the gradient, lying everywhere below the original line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Effect Of Doubling Slit Separation**
From $x = \lambda D / a$, $x$ is inversely proportional to $a$. If $a$ becomes $2a$ with $\lambda$ unchanged, the fringe spacing for any given $D$ is halved: $$x_{new} = \frac{\lambda D}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}x_{old}$$

Step 2: **New Line On The Graph**
Since $G = \lambda / a$, the new gradient is $$G_{new} = \frac{\lambda}{2a} = \frac{G}{2}$$ So draw a straight line from the origin, always below the printed line, reaching only half the $x$-value at the maximum $D$.
